hypothesis: A live condition may make it important to map task changes separately from occupational and employment outcomes.
counter_case: A bounded task map may still miss informal work and unequal power over redesign.

hypothesis: A live condition may make entry routes, review burdens, and distribution across places more important to investigate.
counter_case: These effects may be shaped more by institutions and demand than by the tool.

hypothesis: A future brief may need to retain deliberate non-adoption while evidence and recourse arrangements remain unclear.
counter_case: Waiting can itself impose costs or exclude people from benefits.

hypothesis: This condition may make it important for a team or institution to distinguish a technical marker from a judgement of truth, authorship, or misconduct.
counter_case: Some workflows may not expose or rely on markers at all.

hypothesis: This condition may make accessible processes for questioning an absent, false, or misleading marker more important.
counter_case: A recourse process may not be needed where markers have no decision consequence.

hypothesis: Persistent agent work may make shared practices for commissioning, access boundaries, trace review, and accountable validation more important.
counter_case: Some agents may remain narrow tools that do not alter collaboration or responsibility materially.

hypothesis: Persistent delegation may make institutional permissions, escalation paths, and recourse more important than individual prompting skill alone.
counter_case: In low-risk personal work, formal institutional controls may be irrelevant or burdensome.

hypothesis: Unequal access to time, money, permissions, and technical support may make the participation effects of persistent agents important to investigate.
counter_case: Lower-cost and simpler agent tools may broaden access rather than concentrate it.
